name: Tinɔr / Koro Waci
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Blench, Roger. 2009. The Tinɔr [=Koro Waci] language of Central Nigeria and its affinities. Draft circulated for comment, printout 20 May 2009. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation. 26 pp. (author copy, rogerblench.info via the Internet Archive 2023)
catalog_locator: Section 3 'Phonology', 3.3 'Tones', p.3 (continuing at the top of p.4)
catalog_quote: 3.3 Tones Tinɔr has three level tones, and glide tones that arise from sequences of level tones. The basic conventions are as follows; High ʹ / Mid Unmarked / Low ˋ / Rising ˇ / Falling ˆ. The tone system of Tinɔr is clearly being simplified. High tone is comparatively rare, and words with all three tones now extremely uncommon. Words that are all mid-tone in both singular and plural are very common. Rising and falling tones are very uncommon, but are present. Unlike related languages, long vowels are also uncommon, probably due to greater preservation of segmental morphology, and this is a typical source of glide tones. [printed p.4] All syllables are marked for tone in the present document. Thus any unmarked syllables should be considered mid.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tinɔr (Koro Waci) is described as a tone language with three level tones (High, Mid, Low) and derived rising/falling contours, every syllable bearing tone; the only accessible description makes no statement at all about word stress or accent.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: system 'being simplified' (High rare; all-Mid words very common; contours very uncommon); long vowels uncommon.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns lexical tone on syllables in citation forms of a one-shot elicited wordlist (transcription explicitly 'preliminary'); no word- or phrase-level prominence is discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Blench 2009 describes Tinɔr, i.e. the Waci (Koro Waci) lect, from three Waci Literacy Committee speakers of Kagarko LGA, Kaduna State; he equates Tinor with 'Begbere' (his Fig. 1) and treats Myamya (Miamia) as the second, mutually intelligible lect of the same language - together these are Glottolog begb1241 Begbere-Ejar / ISO bqv. Ethnologue/OLAC also list 'Koro Ache' under bqv, but Ashe is a separate Glottolog language (ashe1269, ISO ahs) with its own Blench 2009 sketch; the SIL 2010 survey's 'Ache dialect' wordlists (Kusam, Dogon Kurmi, Kabara) are from villages Blench lists as Waci/Tinɔr. Gerhardt's 1972/73 'Koro' is probably Tinɔr per Blench.

tone_statements.quote: 3.3 Tones Waci probably has underlyingly two level tones, and glide tones that arise from sequences of level tones. The basic conventions are as follows; High ʹ Mid Unmarked Low ˋ Rising ˇ Falling ˆ The tone system of Waci is clearly being simplified. Mid tone is comparatively rare, and words with all three tones now extremely uncommon. Rising and falling tones are very rare, but are present. Unlike related languages, there are no true long vowels but a few words have doubled vowels usually with dissimilar tones. All syllables are marked for tone in the present document.
tone_statements.locator: Section 3 'Phonology', 3.3 'Tones', p.3 (TOC: '3.3 Tones.. 3'); tone plurals in sec. 4.1 'Nouns', p.6
tone_statements.summary: Probably two underlying level tones (surface H/M/L marking with M rare) plus rare rising/falling contours from tone sequences; syllable is the tone-bearing unit (all syllables marked); lexical tone, and grammatical tone in noun plurals (low prefix ì- raised); system described as simplifying.

sources.note: Sec. 3.3 'Tones' revises the 2009 statement (three level tones) to: probably two underlying level tones, transcribed with High/Mid/Low where Mid is now 'comparatively rare', plus very rare rising and falling glides arising from level-tone sequences; all syllables tone-marked. Sec. 4.1 adds grammatical tone: 'Tone plurals in Waci are almost entirely associated with the i- prefix, which is usually raised from ì- to i-. Stem tones generally [unchanged]' (printed p.6). No mention of stress or accent anywhere in the text.
